text: Everything in this chapter has been building toward one capability: answering, months or years later, exactly what model made a specific decision, what it was trained on, who approved it, and why. In banking, insurance, and healthcare, that isn't a nice to have, it's a legal requirement, and failing to produce the answer is itself a finding.

Frameworks like the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 don't mandate a specific tool, they mandate capabilities. Independent validation before deployment, not after. Ongoing performance monitoring. And documented limitations along with a record of who approved what and when. The registries, gates, and manifests from earlier lessons are how a platform team actually satisfies those capabilities.

A model card is the human-readable counterpart to a reproducibility manifest. Notice it reports evaluation results broken down by region, not just one aggregate number, and it explicitly states what the model is not validated for. A card that only reports one number and says nothing about where the model shouldn't be trusted doesn't satisfy a real review.

Separate from the card, an audit log records every subsequent model-affecting action as an append-only stream. Model registered, alias promoted, and here an automatic rollback with its reason attached. The word immutable matters, this has to be write-once, somewhere entries can't be edited after the fact.

A real audit request looks like show me everything about the model that made decision X. Answering it means walking the audit log to find which version was active at that timestamp, then that version's model card and manifest for what it was trained on, then the approval record showing who signed off. None of the three alone answers the question, together they do.

Auditability means that chain is retrievable on demand, not just technically reconstructible if someone searches long enough. That closes chapter six and the versioning half of this course. Chapter seven turns to platform reliability, SLAs, on-call, and incident response when a model degrades in production.
